name: Bicalutamide

lead: Bicalutamide is a prescription antiandrogen for prostate cancer. Dermatologists sometimes prescribe low doses off-label for female pattern hair loss and excess hair.
Evidence comes from reviews and retrospective data rather than randomised trials, and it has little presence in looksmaxxing forums.

paras: It binds the androgen receptor and blocks testosterone and DHT from activating it, reducing androgen effects on hair follicles.
The label warns of severe and fatal liver injury and requires liver testing. Hot flashes, fatigue and other effects are common in cancer patients; off-label users report liver enzyme elevation.

lead: Bicalutamide (brand name Casodex) is a nonsteroidal androgen-receptor antagonist. Its US label indicates the 50 mg dose in combination with an LHRH analogue for stage D2 metastatic prostate cancer, and states that 150 mg daily is not approved alone or with other treatments in the US [1][2].

Outside that indication, bicalutamide has been used off-label for female pattern hair loss and hirsutism, and in feminising hormone therapy for transgender women [1][3]. A 2025 review describes it as of recent interest in female pattern hair loss, and notes off-label use to improve Sinclair grading [3]. A systematic review of injectable therapies for androgenetic alopecia (AGA) lists bicalutamide among agents studied in mesotherapy [4].

The label warns of severe and fatal liver injury [2]. Forum discussion in the sources is limited: T Nation members have mentioned bicalutamide in androgen-receptor and post-isotretinoin recovery threads [5][6][7].
infobox: 50 mg with LHRH analogue, stage D2 prostate cancer [2]
Off-label, mainly female pattern hair loss [3]

paras: Bicalutamide 50 mg daily with an LHRH analogue is the US-labelled use for metastatic prostate cancer; in the EU the 150 mg dose is also approved as monotherapy for locally advanced disease [1][2]. It features in prostate-cancer trials against newer antiandrogens such as enzalutamide and rezvilutamide, and in trials of androgen deprivation with radiotherapy [8][9][10][11].

A general reference reports off-label use at low doses for female pattern hair loss and hirsutism, with retrospective studies reporting improvement in up to 53 percent of patients, and a 2024 retrospective comparison with spironolactone favouring bicalutamide [1]. The 2025 review describes its anti-androgenic effect on peripheral tissues and its off-label use to improve Sinclair grade in women [3]. Reviews of the hormonal background of hair loss discuss antiandrogen therapies alongside finasteride and spironolactone [12]. It is also used off-label as an antiandrogen in feminising regimens, and for PCOS-related acne and hirsutism [1].

Evidence for hair outcomes is limited to retrospective studies and reviews: a general reference cites retrospective data in female pattern hair loss and notes unapproved use, requiring informed consent and monitoring [1][3]. A 2025 comprehensive review of alopecia drugs examines antiandrogens among treatments for non-scarring alopecia [13]. No randomised trial of bicalutamide for male pattern hair loss was identified; its antiandrogen action in men is the rationale used in discussions, alongside concerns about sexual and breast side effects [1].

The label warns of severe hepatic injury and fatal hepatic failure and advises monitoring transaminases before treatment, at regular intervals for the first four months and periodically after; it also warns of hemorrhage with coumarin anticoagulants [2]. More than 10 percent of patients on bicalutamide plus an LHRH analogue reported hot flashes, pain, asthenia and constipation in trials [2]. A general reference reports elevated liver enzymes in up to 10 percent of off-label users [1].

Bicalutamide competitively inhibits androgen binding to cytosol androgen receptors in target tissue, with the R-enantiomer being active [2][1]. Prostate cancer research has examined androgen-receptor mutations under antiandrogen treatment, including a proposed mechanism for bicalutamide withdrawal syndrome [14][15].

On T Nation, bicalutamide appears mostly in a few threads. One poster recovering from post-isotretinoin symptoms asked whether it could upregulate androgen-receptor expression [5], another mentioned planning to try it before mifepristone [7], and a 2009 poster said it and flutamide are available antiandrogens that carry more oral side effects [16]. No looksmax.org threads on bicalutamide were found.

Large trials exist in prostate cancer [8][9][10][11]. For hair loss, no randomised trial was identified; evidence consists of reviews and retrospective data [1][3]. A systematic review of mesotherapy for AGA included bicalutamide among agents studied, reporting mostly mild adverse events across injectable therapies [4].

lore.intro: Bicalutamide is mentioned occasionally on T Nation as an experimental antiandrogen, mainly in recovery and androgen-receptor discussions [5][7][16].

claims.claim: Bicalutamide might upregulate androgen receptors and help recover from post-isotretinoin or post-finasteride problems.
